en: Sutta Nipāta 3.3 Subhāsitasutta Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken, not ill-spoken, and is both blameless and irreproachable to the wise.”
"By which four?

Here, monks, a monk speaks only what is well-spoken, not what is ill-spoken; he speaks only the Dhamma, not what is non-Dhamma; he speaks only what is pleasing, not what is displeasing; he speaks only the truth, not what is false.
It is by possessing these four factors, monks, that speech is well-spoken, not ill-spoken, and is blameless and beyond reproach to the wise."
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
"The virtuous say that well-spoken words are supreme."
“Speak the Dhamma, not what is contrary to the Dhamma—that is the second;
speak what is pleasing, not what is unpleasing—that is the third;
speak the truth, not what is false—that is the fourth.”

Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
“An inspiration has come to me, Blessed One; an inspiration has come to me, Sugata.
“Let it inspire you, Vaṅgīsa,” the Blessed One said.
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
“One should speak only that speech by which one does not burn oneself;”
And that which does not harm others—
that indeed is well-spoken speech.
One should speak only words that are pleasing.
That speech which is welcomed with acclaim,
which, without taking up evil,
speaks what is pleasing to others.
Truth indeed is the deathless word;
this is the eternal Dhamma.
In truth, in the goal, and in the Dhamma—
The virtuous say that they are well-established in whatever word the Buddha speaks for the attainment of the secure state of Nibbāna.
For the making an end of suffering—
this indeed is the supreme among speeches.
Thus ends the third sutta, “Well-Spoken.”
